title: Build-up of US copper stocks leading to apparent market tightness
gist: Copper is trading near record highs (~USD 15,000/t) despite an actual market surplus, because huge stockpiling flows into the US (driven by tariff-front-running) are removing material from global price formation and making the market feel far tighter than it really is; Benchmark warns this apparent deficit could reverse fast if US tariff policy changes.

insights.claim: Copper prices hit record highs repeatedly through 2026 and were approaching USD 15,000/t as of 10 September 2026, even though 2025 saw a multi-year-high surplus and 2026 is also tracking as a broad surplus.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Price action is diverging sharply from fundamentals-implied surplus; investors should treat the copper rally as a positioning/flow story, not a pure supply-deficit story.
insights.quote: Copper prices have hit record high after record high in 2026, and are approaching USD 15,000/t as of 10 September.

insights.claim: Benchmark assessed that in 2025 the copper market 'felt' about 700kt tighter than the actual surplus because so much copper flowed into US stockpiles, and expects the 2026 perceived tightness to be roughly 880kt greater than the true surplus.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Gives a quantified gap between headline sentiment and underlying balance (700kt in 2025, ~880kt in 2026) that traders can use to size how much of the price move is stockpile-driven distortion versus real scarcity.
insights.quote: Benchmark assessed the market as “feeling” 700kt tighter in 2025 than the actual surplus, and Benchmark expects the perceived tightness to be 880kt lower than the actual surplus in 2026.
insights.locator: second paragraph, 'In 2025, so much copper went to the US'

insights.claim: Copper stockpiling into the US is not genuine end-market demand; it functions like demand for global price-formation purposes because the material becomes unavailable to the rest of the world, but it is not being consumed.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Distinguishes real consumption growth from inventory-hoarding; investors betting on a structural copper demand story should separate this stockpile effect out of their models.
insights.quote: Stock build out in the US is not real “demand”.

insights.claim: In 2026, the apparent copper deficit (after netting out excess US stockpiles) is roughly the same size as the deficit seen in 2022, and this repeated string of apparent/actual deficits is compounding with other bullish factors to keep pushing prices to new highs.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: Benchmarking the 2026 apparent deficit against the known 2022 deficit gives investors a concrete historical yardstick for how tight conditions currently look on paper.

insights.claim: Of 994kt of global visible copper inventory across the LME, CME and SHFE exchanges, 800kt (roughly 80%) is physically located in the United States, per Benchmark's Copper Service.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: An investor tracking exchange inventories for copper signal should note that headline visible-stock levels are geographically skewed to the US and don't represent globally available supply.
insights.quote: Of the 994kt of global visible inventory, 800kt is in the US, as assessed by Benchmark’s Copper Service.
insights.locator: paragraph with Albert Mackenzie quote on invisible stock

insights.claim: Beyond the visible exchange stocks, there is a large amount of invisible (off-exchange, unreported) copper stock sitting in the US, according to Benchmark copper analyst Albert Mackenzie.
insights.speaker: Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark
insights.so_what: True US copper inventories, and thus the true global surplus, are likely larger than visible-exchange data suggests — a caution against relying solely on LME/CME/SHFE reported stocks.
insights.quote: There is a large amount of invisible stock in the US but even if we look at visible inventories on the three major exchanges – the LME, CME, and SHFE – we see material geographically focused in the US

themes.theme: Tariff policy as the swing factor

insights.claim: The US copper stockpile has not yet been consumed or turned into finished products, meaning it remains available to re-enter global price formation if conditions change.
insights.speaker: Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark
insights.so_what: This is a latent supply overhang: watch for signs the stockpiled cathode starts flowing back out, which would be bearish for price even without new mine supply.
insights.quote: What goes up must come down though, and this material has not been turned into anything yet, so the material could once again become part of price formation

insights.claim: Whether the artificial copper tightness persists or reverses hinges on the next US tariff update; if the US moves to reduce cathode import flows, the previously stockpiled material could flood back into global markets and make the market artificially loose.
insights.speaker: Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark
insights.so_what: A single, near-term identifiable catalyst (a US tariff decision on copper/cathode) could flip the market from apparent deficit to apparent surplus — investors should watch US trade policy announcements as the key risk event for a copper price reversal.
insights.quote: The whole picture hinges on the next tariff update, and if the US makes a move that leads to a reduction in cathode flows to the US the material that has turned the market into an artificial deficit could make the market artificially looser in future.

insights.claim: Beyond the US stockpile-driven apparent deficit, copper prices are also being pushed higher by AI-related bullishness, long-term fears about future copper supply, and a market narrative around supply disruptions.
insights.speaker: Benchmark Team
insights.so_what: AI infrastructure buildout (data centers, grid, power) is cited as a demand narrative supporting copper prices — relevant for investors positioning in copper miners or AI-infrastructure-linked commodity trades.
insights.quote: These other factors driving higher prices include AI bullishness, long-term fears about copper supply, and a narrative of supply disruptions for example.

insights.claim: Financial players are increasingly spilling over into metal markets, contributing to broad-based upward pressure on base metal prices generally, not just copper.
insights.speaker: Albert Mackenzie, copper analyst at Benchmark
insights.so_what: Signals that part of the current metals rally is a financialization/flow phenomenon (speculative or macro-hedging capital), which can reverse quickly and independent of physical fundamentals — a risk factor for anyone long base metals on a pure fundamentals thesis.
insights.quote: Beyond that, we seem to see some financial players overspill into metal markets and this is pushing up base metals across the board
